englishChanges.before: Now, to those who condemned me, I want to make a prophecy — for in the hour of death, people are gifted with prophetic power. I tell you, my executioners: the moment I'm gone, a punishment far heavier than what you've given me will fall on you. You killed me because you wanted to avoid being questioned, to avoid giving an account of your lives. But it won't work out that way. There will be more people questioning you than before — people I've been holding back. They're younger and will be harsher, and you'll be even more offended. If you think killing people will stop them from criticizing your lives, you're wrong. That escape route is neither possible nor honorable. The easiest and noblest path is not to silence others but to improve yourselves. That is my prophecy to those who condemned me.
englishChanges.after: Now I want to prophesy to those who condemned me, for I am about to die, and at the hour of death people are given prophetic power. I predict that immediately after my death, you, my killers, will face a far heavier punishment than the one you have imposed on me. You killed me to escape being called to account for your lives. But things will turn out quite differently. More people will call you to account than do now, people I have held back until this point. They are younger, will show you less consideration, and will offend you more. If you think killing people can prevent someone from criticizing your bad lives, you are mistaken. That escape is neither possible nor honorable. The easiest and noblest course is not to disable others but to improve yourselves. That is my prophecy, before I depart, to the judges who condemned me.

englishChanges.before: To my friends who voted to acquit me, I'd like to talk about what has just happened, while we have time before I go to my death. Stay with me a moment — we can talk while it's still possible. I want to tell you something remarkable. Throughout my life, my divine sign — that inner voice — has constantly opposed me, even in trivial matters, whenever I was about to make a mistake. Yet today, facing what most people consider the ultimate evil, the sign didn't oppose me at all — not when I left home this morning, not when I came to court, not during anything I said. In the past, it has often stopped me mid-sentence. But today it raised no objection to anything I said or did. What do I make of this? I'll tell you: it suggests that what has happened to me is actually good. Those of us who think death is evil must be wrong. My sign would certainly have stopped me if I had been heading toward harm.
englishChanges.after: My friends who would have acquitted me, I would also like to speak with you about what has happened, while the officials are busy and before I go to the place where I must die. Stay a little, so we can talk while there is time. You are my friends, and I want to show you how I understand what has happened to me. My judges, for you I can truly call judges, I want to tell you something remarkable. Until now, the divine voice within me has constantly stopped me, even over trivial matters, when I was about to make a mistake. Now I face what most people consider the final and worst evil. Yet the sign did not oppose me when I left home this morning, on my way to court, or during my speech, whatever I was about to say. In the past, it has often stopped me in the middle of speaking. But in this case it has opposed nothing I said or did. How do I explain its silence? I will tell you. It is a sign that what has happened to me is good, and that those of us who think death is an evil are mistaken. The usual sign would surely have stopped me if I had been heading toward something bad rather than good.

englishChanges.before: Consider it this way, and there's strong reason to hope that death is good. Death is one of two things: either it's a state of complete nothingness and unconsciousness, or it's a journey to another place where the dead reside. If it's dreamless sleep, then death is an extraordinary gain. Think about it: if someone picked the night in which they slept so soundly they didn't even dream, and compared it with all the other nights and days of their life — even a great king would find very few days or nights more pleasant than that one. If death is like that, it's pure gain — eternity becomes a single peaceful night. But if death is a journey to another place where all the dead gather, what could be better? Imagine arriving where the pretend judges of this world have no power, and finding the true judges — Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and every other righteous soul. Wouldn't that journey be worth making?
englishChanges.after: Let us consider it another way, and we will see strong grounds for hoping that death is good. It must be one of two things: either a state of nothingness and complete unconsciousness, or, as people say, a change in which the soul moves from this world to another. If there is no consciousness, only sleep undisturbed even by dreams, death would be an indescribable gain. Suppose someone chose a night of completely dreamless sleep and compared it with all the other days and nights of his life. How many had been better and more pleasant than that one? I think not just an ordinary person but even the great king would find few among all the others. If death is like that, I say dying is a gain, for eternity is then just one night. But if death is a journey to another place where, as people say, all the dead live, what could be better, my friends and judges? If the traveler arriving in the world below escapes this world's self-proclaimed judges and finds the true judges said to give judgment there, Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and other sons of gods who lived justly, then that journey would be worth making.

englishChanges.before: What would you give to talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer? If this is true, let me die again and again! I'd find it wonderful to meet Palamedes, Ajax, and every hero who suffered an unjust death — comparing my experience with theirs would be endlessly fascinating. Best of all, I could continue doing what I do now: examining people. What would you give to question the leaders of the Trojan War, or Odysseus, or Sisyphus, or countless others — men and women both? The joy of conversing with them and examining them would be beyond measure. And in that world, they certainly don't execute people for asking questions. The dead are not only happier than the living but, if what we're told is true, they're immortal.
englishChanges.after: What would anyone not give to talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer? If that is true, let me die again and again. I myself would find it wonderful to meet and speak with Palamedes, Ajax son of Telamon, and other ancient heroes who died through an unjust judgment. Comparing my sufferings with theirs would give me no small pleasure. Above all, I could continue investigating true and false knowledge there as here, discovering who is wise and who merely thinks himself wise without being so. What would anyone not give, my judges, to question the leader of the great expedition against Troy, or Odysseus, Sisyphus, and countless others, both men and women! What boundless delight it would be to talk with them and ask them questions! In that other world, people are certainly not put to death for asking questions. Besides being happier than we are, they are immortal, if what people say is true.

englishChanges.before: So be of good cheer about death, my judges, and remember this truth: no evil can befall a good person, in life or in death. The gods do not neglect such a person. What has happened to me hasn't happened by accident. I see clearly that it was better for me to die now and be released from trouble. That's why my divine sign never stopped me today. I bear no anger toward my accusers or those who condemned me. They haven't actually harmed me, even though they didn't intend to help me. For that, I may gently criticize them.
englishChanges.after: So be of good cheer about death, my judges, and know for certain that no evil can befall a good person, either in life or after death. That is why the sign did not intervene. For the same reason, I am not angry with those who condemned or accused me. They have done me no harm, although they did not intend to do me any good either. For that I may gently reproach them.

englishChanges.before: But I do have one favor to ask. When my sons are grown, I ask you, my friends, to give them the same trouble I've given you — if they seem to care more about money or anything else than about virtue, or if they pretend to be something they're not. Challenge them as I've challenged you, for not caring about what truly matters and for thinking they're someone when they're nothing. If you do this, both I and my sons will have been treated justly.

If they pretend to be something when they are nothing, rebuke them as I have rebuked you: for neglecting what they should care about and thinking themselves something when they are nothing. If you do this, you will have treated both me and my sons justly.
